From body to base pair.

Follow one cancer from a shadow on a scan down to a single changed letter of DNA. Each scale answers a different question. Where is it? What tissue did it come from? Which proteins does it make? Part one · How a cancer begins

Cells, genes and the controls that keep tissues in balance, and what happens when those controls fail. No background needed.

i

Chapter oneScale · 10⁻⁵ m

Thirty trillion cells, one set of instructions.

Nearly every cell in your body carries the same DNA: about two metres of it, folded into a nucleus a hundredth of a millimetre across. Cells read different parts of it to become skin, blood or bone. Cancer starts when some of those instructions change and a cell stops following the rules that keep a tissue in balance.

Gene → message → protein

How a cell reads one gene.

This is a real stretch of the EGFR gene, the gene changed in Case A at the top of the page. Step through it, then switch on the mutation and watch one changed letter reach the protein.

The cell cycle

Division runs through checkpoints. Cancer cells run through them anyway.

ii

Chapter twoScale · genes → clones

A stuck accelerator and cut brakes.

Genes that control growth come in two broad kinds. Oncogenes work like an accelerator: one faulty copy can jam it down. Tumour suppressor genes work like brakes: usually both copies have to fail. Most cancers need several such hits, collected over years, in one line of cells.

Two copies of every gene

Hit a copy and see what changes.

You inherit one copy of each gene from each parent. Click a copy to mutate it.

Selection inside a tissue

Grow a clone.

Each square is a cell in the lining of an organ, sitting on its basement membrane. Normal cells divide only to replace cells that die. When a cell picks up a hit, every daughter inherits it. A cell with the right combination outgrows its neighbours, and its descendants form a clone. Choose a hit and click a cell, or let mutations arise at random.

A teaching model. Real tissues hold billions of cells and take years; mutation rates here are accelerated enormously so selection is visible in a minute. Colours mark how many hits a cell carries.

What a pathologist might call it

Normal

Hit to add when you click a cell

    Drivers and passengers. A typical tumour carries thousands of mutations. Most are passengers that change nothing. A small number, often four or five in a common adult cancer, are drivers that give the clone its edge. Peter Nowell described cancer as this kind of step-by-step evolution in 1976.

    Because the clone keeps evolving, cells in different parts of one tumour can differ. That is one reason a treatment can shrink most of a tumour and still leave a resistant group behind.

    Why inherited cancers appear earlier. Someone born with one faulty copy of a brake gene, such as BRCA1 or RB1, already carries the first hit in every cell. One more chance hit can be enough, so their cancers tend to start younger and sometimes on both sides of the body. Alfred Knudson's 1971 study of the eye cancer retinoblastoma first set out this two-hit idea.
    iii

    Chapter threeScale · cell behaviour

    The hallmarks: what a cell must gain to become a cancer.

    In 2000 Douglas Hanahan and Robert Weinberg proposed that most, perhaps all, cancers acquire a shared set of capabilities. They updated the framework in 2011, and Hanahan extended it in 2022. It also maps cleanly onto treatment: many modern drugs aim at a single hallmark.

    iv

    Chapter fourScale · tissue over years

    Becoming cancer, one boundary at a time.

    Carcinomas, the most common cancers, begin in an epithelium, the cell sheet that lines a surface. What separates a precursor from a cancer, and a cancer from a metastasis, is usually a boundary that has been crossed.

    The metastatic cascade

    Six steps, each a filter that most cells fail.

    Large numbers of tumour cells can enter the blood, yet only a tiny fraction found a metastasis. Each step selects for cells that can survive the next environment. In 1889 Stephen Paget called this the seed and soil problem: where a cancer spreads depends on both the cell and the organ it reaches.

      Where cancers travel

      Common sites of spread are not random.

      v

      Chapter fiveScale · tissue of origin

      A cancer is named for the cell it came from.

      "Cancer" covers more than a hundred diseases. The first split is whether a growth is benign or malignant. The second is the kind of cell it started in, which sets its name, how it behaves and how it is treated.

      Benign or malignant

      Both are tumours. Only one invades.

      "Tumour" means a swelling or mass, benign or malignant. Hippocrates called malignant tumours karkinos, Greek for crab, probably because the finger-like projections spreading from a tumour called a crab to mind. The Roman writer Celsus translated it into Latin as cancer. The physician Galen later used oncos, Greek for swelling, which gives us oncology.

      Families of cancer

      Ten families by tissue of origin.

      Reading the name

      Tissue + ending = diagnosis.

      Most tumour names join a word for the tissue to an ending. -oma on its own usually means benign. -carcinoma means malignant and from a lining (epithelium). -sarcoma means malignant and from connective tissue. Pick a tissue and a behaviour.

      Exceptions. A few "-oma" names are malignant by convention: melanoma, lymphoma, seminoma, mesothelioma and myeloma. Glioma covers a range from slow-growing to aggressive. When in doubt, the report will say "malignant" or "benign".

      Part two · Causes, detection and scale

      Where the mutations come from, how much can be prevented, how a tumour grows from one cell, and how many people cancer touches.

      vi

      Chapter sixScale · a lifetime

      Where the hits come from, and which ones we can avoid.

      Every cancer needs mutations. Some come from the unavoidable wear of copying DNA over a lifetime. Others are caused by tobacco, sunlight, alcohol, infections or body weight, and those can be reduced. A few are inherited.

      Five sources of damage

      Each leaves its own fingerprint in the DNA.

      Different causes change DNA in different ways. Sequencing a tumour can reveal these patterns, called mutational signatures, years after the exposure.

        Age

        Most cancers are found in later life.

        Hits pile up with every year and every division, and the body's defences weaken with age. Rates climb from fewer than 26 new cancers per 100,000 people a year under age 20 to more than 1,000 per 100,000 from age 60. Half of all US cancers are diagnosed at 67 or older. Childhood cancers are rare and mostly different diseases, usually arising from developing tissue rather than from decades of damage.

        What is preventable

        Four in ten cancers in US adults are linked to risks that can be changed.

        Levers

        What lowers risk.

        vii

        Chapter sevenScale · 10⁻⁵ → 10⁻¹ m

        From one cell to a lump you can feel.

        A tumour that doubles in size again and again grows invisibly for most of its life. That hidden stretch is why screening exists: to find some cancers, or their precursors, before they cause symptoms.

        Drag to double

        Doublings30
        Cells
        Diameter · weight

        An idealised curve. Real tumours do not double on a timetable. Many cells die along the way, growth usually slows as a tumour gets bigger, and doubling times range from weeks to years. The arithmetic still holds: a 1 cm tumour has already passed about 30 of the 40 doublings that would take it to a kilogram. The usual rule of thumb is a billion cells per gram; because tumours also contain blood vessels and supporting tissue, the true number of cancer cells may be nearer a hundred million.

        Screening

        Tests for people without symptoms.

        These are the US Preventive Services Task Force recommendations for people at average risk. Other countries choose different ages and intervals, and people at higher risk often start earlier.

        Symptoms worth checking

        Most have harmless causes. Persistent ones deserve a look.

          In plain wordsA symptom that is new, unexplained and lasts more than a few weeks is a reason to see a doctor. It is rarely cancer. When it is, finding it earlier usually means more treatment options.

          Chapter eightScale · populations

          Twenty million diagnoses a year, and they are not alike.

          Common cancers are not always the deadliest. Comparing new cases with deaths shows which cancers are usually caught and treated, and which are usually found late or resist treatment.

          20.0Mnew cancer diagnoses worldwide in 2022

          Worldwide estimates for 2022, both sexes, 14 sites. Colorectum excludes anus. Hover or tap a row for exact counts. IARC has since published GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates; the overall picture is similar.

          Deaths per case is the mortality-to-incidence ratio. It is a crude, population-level signal: a ratio near 1 means that, across the world, almost as many people die of the cancer each year as are diagnosed with it. Pancreatic, liver and oesophageal cancers sit near the top because they are often found late and are hard to treat. Thyroid and prostate cancers sit near the bottom because many are slow-growing and many are detected early.

          Not a survival rate. The ratio compares two counts from the same year, which come from different people. It also hides large differences between countries. For a person's outlook, stage-specific survival (Chapter ix) is far more informative.

          ix

          Chapter nineScale · 10⁻¹ m

          Five organs, five ways to measure extent.

          The T in TNM is measured differently in each organ. In the bowel and bladder it is depth through the wall. In the lung and breast it is mostly size. In the prostate it is whether the tumour has broken out of the gland. Move the tumour and watch its category change.

          Prostate cancer in depth

          Grade, risk group and disease state: the three labels in every prostate note.

          The explorer above measures extent. Prostate cancer notes add three more labels that decide treatment: how abnormal the glands look (Gleason pattern, score and Grade Group), how likely the cancer is to progress when PSA, stage and grade are combined (risk group), and where the patient stands in a long course of treatment (disease state). The next four blocks build each label from the tissue up.

          Prostate in depth · 1 of 4

          Gleason patterns: grading the architecture.

          A pathologist grades prostate cancer by how well the tumour cells still build glands. Normal prostate glands are round or branched tubes with an open lumen, wrapped in pink stroma. The more a tumour loses that plan, the higher the pattern. Pick a pattern, then one of its forms, and look at what the pathologist looks at.

          Patterns 1 and 2 are gone in practice. Gleason's original scheme had five patterns. Since the ISUP consensus conferences of 2005 and 2014, patterns 1 and 2 are essentially never assigned, above all on needle biopsy, so the lowest score in use is 3+3=6. That is why a "Gleason 6" tumour is the lowest grade, not the middle of a 2 to 10 scale.

          Prostate in depth · 2 of 4

          From patterns to a score to a Grade Group.

          A tumour usually holds more than one pattern. The Gleason score adds the primary pattern (the most common) to the secondary pattern. The ISUP Grade Group then folds the nine possible sums into five groups that behave differently. Set how much of each pattern the tumour contains and see what the two sampling rules produce.

          Tumour composition

          Pattern 3 (the rest)80%

          Try an example

          Why 3+4=7 and 4+3=7 are different tumours

          Both add up to 7, but they do not behave alike. In 3+4 (Grade Group 2) most of the tumour is still well-formed pattern 3 and pattern 4 is the minority. In 4+3 (Grade Group 3) the majority is pattern 4. Large outcome studies, after prostatectomy and after radiotherapy, show 4+3 doing worse than 3+4. A single "Gleason 7" hid that gap. This is the main reason Grade Groups were introduced in 2014.

          The same logic runs inside each group. A 3+4 tumour with 5% pattern 4 and one with 45% pattern 4 share a Grade Group but not a prognosis. So ISUP and GUPS both ask for the percentage of pattern 4 on biopsy whenever the score is 7.

          Cribriform and intraductal carcinoma

          Cribriform
          Sieve-like nests of tumour cells. Always pattern 4 or higher. Linked in many cohorts to a worse outcome than other pattern 4 forms, so ISUP (2019) and GUPS (2019) ask pathologists to report whether it is present.
          Intraductal carcinoma
          Tumour cells filling and expanding the existing prostate ducts, with the duct wall still intact. Often sits beside high-grade invasive cancer. Reported as "intraductal carcinoma" (IDC-P). Many guidelines treat it as an adverse feature that argues against active surveillance.
          Where they differ
          With invasive cancer present, ISUP 2019 lets the intraductal part be graded like invasive tumour (comedonecrosis counts as pattern 5). GUPS 2019 grades only the invasive part and comments on the intraductal part. A joint GUPS and ISUP consultation published in 2026 now favours including intraductal carcinoma in the grade when it sits with invasive cancer, and not grading pure intraductal carcinoma. Reports from different years can therefore differ.

          Biopsy rule, prostatectomy rule, and where the societies differ

          QuestionISUP 2014 and 2019GUPS 2019
          Needle biopsy: which patterns make the score?Most common pattern plus the highest-grade pattern, whatever its amount. A third, higher pattern is not called tertiary on biopsy.Same approach.
          Radical prostatectomy: which patterns make the score?Most common plus second most common. A higher-grade third pattern under about 5% is added as a note ("tertiary" pattern 4 or 5) and not to the sum.Same sum. Uses "minor" for small patterns and keeps "tertiary" only for a pattern 5 under 5% in a Grade Group 2 or 3 tumour.

          Prostate in depth · 3 of 4

          Risk groups: combining PSA, stage and grade.

          No single number says how dangerous a localised prostate cancer is. Three questions together do: how high is the PSA, how far has the tumour grown (clinical T), and how abnormal is it (Grade Group). Risk tools combine them into a few groups that guide treatment, from active surveillance to radiotherapy with long hormone therapy. Three systems are in common use and they do not always agree. Enter one case and compare.

          Learning tool, not a clinical calculator. NCCN revises its prostate guideline several times a year. In 2025 it redefined very high risk, and in 2026 it removed the very-low-risk group. The 2026 mode follows those reported changes; check the current NCCN table before relying on any group, and use the NCCN and EAU documents for real decisions.

          Case inputs

          Try a case

          Optional fields feed only the earlier NCCN definitions: PSA density and core involvement for "very low", cores with Grade Group 4 or 5 for "very high". All three systems use the highest Grade Group found on biopsy.

          Prostate in depth · 4 of 4

          States of prostate cancer over time.

          Prostate cancer is often a decades-long illness, and a note's wording changes with each phase. Clinicians describe the phase with a state: whether there is cancer on scans, whether treatment has been given, and whether the cancer still responds to testosterone-lowering therapy. The state, more than the original stage, decides what is offered next. The curve shows PSA through one illustrative course. Click a state, or use the buttons beneath.

          Old words, new words and traps

          You may readIt meansWatch for
          Hormone-sensitive, castration-sensitive, hormone-naive (HSPC, CSPC)Still responds to testosterone lowering. "Naive" strictly means no hormone therapy yet.Documents mix "naive" and "sensitive". A patient on ADT with a falling PSA is sensitive but not naive.
          Castration-resistant (CRPC); "castrate-resistant" is a spelling variantProgression despite testosterone below 50 ng/dL (1.7 nmol/L).Many notes write "CRPC" without a testosterone value. Check that castration was actually achieved.
          Hormone-refractory, androgen-independent (HRPC, AIPC)Obsolete names for CRPC.They imply the cancer no longer needs androgen signalling. It usually still does, which is why newer hormone drugs work. Found in older notes and patient summaries.
          De novo, synchronous, M1 at diagnosisMetastatic when first diagnosed.Opposite of "recurrent", "metachronous" or "relapsed" metastatic disease after earlier local treatment.
          Biochemical recurrence, PSA failure, PSA relapseA rising PSA after radical treatment, without proven metastases."PSA progression" on ADT means something else: it is part of the CRPC definition.
          ARPI, ARSI, NHA, NHT, "second-generation antiandrogen"Androgen receptor pathway inhibitors: enzalutamide, apalutamide, darolutamide, abiraterone.Abiraterone blocks testosterone production; the other three block the receptor. NCCN now uses "ARPI" for these drugs.

          Chapter tenScale · notation

          The grammar of a stage.

          A string like ypT2 N1a M0 packs in when the assessment was made, what evidence it rests on, and how far the cancer reached. Type or paste one to see it taken apart.

          Try
          cClinical. Examination, imaging and biopsy before treatment.
          pPathological. Adds the resection specimen when its requirements are met.
          yAssessed after initial systemic or radiation therapy.
          rRecurrence, staged after a disease-free interval.
          aDetermined at autopsy.

          No stage group is calculated here. Turning T, N and M into a stage (I to IV) needs the organ's current AJCC tables, and for some organs also grade, biomarkers or PSA. The organ notes summarise AJCC 8th-edition concepts, plus Version 9 for lung, in plain words.

          xi

          Chapter elevenScale · 10⁰ → 10⁻¹⁰ m

          Every instrument sees one slice of scale.

          A PET scan can survey the whole body but cannot resolve anything smaller than a few millimetres. A microscope resolves details of a fraction of a micrometre but sees only a sliver of tissue. Diagnosis means stitching their views together.

          Molecular imaging

          The tracer decides what lights up.

          A PET scanner does not photograph tissue. It records where radioactive atoms went. Each atom is attached to a molecule, the tracer, and the molecule decides the destination: glucose-like molecules go where sugar is burned, PSMA binders go where PSMA sits, hormone look-alikes go where the oestrogen receptor sits. So the same body gives a different picture with every tracer, and a bright spot has to be read against that tracer's normal map. The PET-CT row above covers how fine a detail PET can resolve. This block covers what each tracer reports.

          Choose a tracer. The figure is a maximum-intensity projection (MIP), the way a PET report's key image is drawn: the scanner collapses the whole 3D scan onto one flat anterior view, keeping the brightest voxel along each line of sight. The patient's right is on the viewer's left. More ink means more uptake: darker on a light page, brighter on a dark page.

          Reading the words

          How a PET report describes uptake.

          A PET report has a small vocabulary that sounds like measurement and is mostly judgement. Three questions sit behind nearly every sentence. Where is the uptake, and is that a place where this tracer is normally taken up? How much compared with a stated reference? What shape: one spot, several, or a smear? The tools below take those three apart.

          Word or phraseWhat the writer meansWhat it does not tell you
          uptake, accumulationTracer is present in the tissue. Neutral until an adjective or number is added.Whether the tissue is benign or malignant.
          avid, tracer-avid, FDG-avid, PSMA-avidUptake clearly above its background. The reader is judging, often against a reference organ.A threshold. Avid is not a synonym for cancer: infection and healing bone are avid too.
          hypermetabolicFDG only: glucose use above the surroundings.It is meaningless for a PSMA or receptor tracer, which does not measure metabolism.
          expressionThe biology the writer infers from the uptake, as in "PSMA expression". High uptake suggests more target.Uptake is a proxy. Blood flow, size and kidney clearance also move it.
          non-avid, no abnormal uptakeUptake is not above background.That the lesion is benign. Tiny lesions and low-uptake tumours can be non-avid.
          photopenic, coldLess uptake than the surroundings.The cause. Necrosis, a cyst, surgery or an implant can all leave a cold area.
          physiological, normal biodistributionUptake expected in a healthy organ for this tracer.That every bright spot at that site is normal. A ganglion can sit beside a node.
          mild, moderate, intenseRelative intensity words.Relative to what. Good reports add "greater than liver" or an SUV.
          focus (foci), focalA small, round, discrete spot. Several of them are "multifocal".The size of the lesion. A focus is a pattern, not a measurement.
          diffuseSpread through a whole organ or tissue.Usually reactive or physiological (thyroiditis, marrow after growth factors), but marrow infiltration can look the same.
          equivocal, indeterminateThe reader cannot call it benign or malignant.A probability. Look for the follow-up advice that comes with it.

          Why SUVmax does not travel

          • Scanner and software. Calibration, reconstruction and filtering change the hottest voxel. Harmonisation programmes such as EARL exist because sites differ.
          • Timing. Uptake keeps changing after injection, so a scan at 60 minutes and one at 90 minutes disagree.
          • Patient. Weight, fat, kidney function and, for FDG, blood glucose change the number.
          • Lesion size. Small lesions read low because of partial-volume blurring. One noisy voxel can read high.
          • Tracer. An SUV of 6 on one PSMA agent is not an SUV of 6 on another, and means nothing against FDG.

          The fix is a reference organ. Compare the lesion with blood pool, liver or parotid gland on the same scan. The ratio survives a change of scanner far better than the raw number. That is the idea behind the PROMISE score below.

          Describe one lesion.

          Pick a shape and slide the SUVmax. The reference organs differ between two synthetic scans, so the same SUVmax can give a different intensity score.

          PSMA-RADS

          One lesion at a time: how likely is prostate cancer?

          PSMA-RADS sorts each PSMA-avid finding by how likely it is to be prostate cancer. Version 1.0 appeared in 2018. Version 2.0 (published 2023) simplified category 1, added 5T for treated lesions and lets some equivocal lesions move up in widespread disease. Reports should say which version they use. Select a category.

          Bar length shows the order of the categories only. It is not a probability.

          PROMISE miTNM

          Intensity score and a TNM for PSMA PET.

          PROMISE (Prostate Cancer Molecular Imaging Standardized Evaluation) does two jobs. The miPSMA score grades how intense a lesion is against reference organs. The miTNM lists where disease is, with an mi prefix for molecular imaging. Version 2 (2023) is the current one. Type a string or choose an example.

          Which version? Older reports and papers use PROMISE version 1 (2018), which wrote pelvic nodes as miN1a (one region) and miN1b (several regions). Version 2 writes miN1 and miN2, so "miN1a" signals a version 1 report. Treat any notation as a pointer to the report's own words until you know the version. An international Delphi consensus (SPARC, European Urology 2026) recommended using miPSMA for expression, PROMISE miTNM for staging and reporting SUVmax by region rather than as one number.

          A rising PSA, and a seven-millimetre node.

          This invented report follows a man whose PSA began to rise after prostatectomy. Select any highlighted phrase to see what it means and how it is easily misread.

          How certain is the radiologist?

          Hedging words carry a probability, but nobody agrees which.

          Radiologists rarely write "cancer". They write "suspicious for" or "cannot be excluded". Those phrases carry a rough probability, and studies show readers and writers disagree about it. A lexicon used at Memorial Sloan Kettering ties five terms to anchor values; the ACR Commission on Quality and Safety (2025) reviewed the problem and recommends more consistent use. The chart shows those anchors as solid bars and the likely spread of real-world reading as pale bars. Select a phrase.

          When the hedge has a number: structured categories.

          Structured reporting systems fix the meaning. Each ACR "RADS" system assigns a category to a finding and ties it to a likely next step. The categories look alike across systems but the numbers inside them do not. Choose a system.

          xii

          Chapter twelveScale · 10⁻⁹ m

          A biomarker is a measurement. First ask what was measured.

          Genes, RNA and proteins sit at different depths in the cell, and each is read by a different test. Many errors in reading reports come from treating a protein result and a gene result as the same thing.

          Result states

          Six words that are easy to misread.

          Detected

          The target was found and reported under the assay's rules. Whether it matters still depends on the exact variant and the cancer.

          Not detected

          A valid test did not find the target within what it covers and how sensitive it is. This is a bounded negative.

          Pending

          The result is not final. It is not negative, and decisions may wait for it.

          Indeterminate

          The signal cannot be classified with confidence. The report may suggest a different test.

          Insufficient

          The sample did not meet the test's requirements. This is a technical failure, not a biological answer.

          Not performed

          No test was done. No conclusion either way.

          Molecular reports · Variant names

          Reading variant notation (HGVS).

          The cards above say which genes matter. A molecular report says which exact change was found, and it follows a standard grammar from the Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS). The grammar has three parts: which reference sequence, which level of the molecule, and what happened at which position.

          Chapter i showed one variant at codon level. Here the same grammar is taken apart. Type any variant, or choose an example.

          Try

          Six prefixes you will meet

          g.
          Genomic: a position along a chromosome. It depends on the genome build, for example NC_000007.14:g.55191822T>G on build GRCh38.
          c.
          Coding DNA: counted from the start codon of one transcript, skipping introns. This is the level most reports lead with.
          n.
          Non-coding transcript: the same idea for genes that do not make protein.
          r.
          RNA: written in lower case, with u for uracil.
          p.
          Protein: amino acid numbers. A predicted change is written in parentheses.
          m.
          Mitochondrial DNA. A seventh prefix, o., is for other circular genomes and is rarely seen in human reports.

          In documents

          One variant, many spellings.

          The same change can be written several ways in different documents. Levels differ (DNA or protein). Letter codes differ (L or Leu). Transcripts and genome builds change the numbers. Older systems name the same event differently. Different DNA changes can also produce one protein change, and a lab may give the protein change only.

          Shorthand forms and what they stand for

          exon 19 delA class of in-frame deletions in exon 19, not one variant.c.2235_2249del or c.2236_2250del, both p.(Glu746_Ala750del), and othersMany different DNA deletions are grouped under this phrase.

          Exon numbers also vary. Some labs count only coding exons, and older systems skip exons. TP53 c.916C>T is exon 8 in the common numbering but coding exon 7 in some reports. BRCA1 c.5266dup is exon 19 in the current RefSeq numbering and exon 20 in older documents.

          Molecular reports · Variant types

          Variant types: what changed, and which test can see it.

          A variant name tells you where. A variant type tells you what kind of change it is, and the type decides which test can find it. Select any box. Boxes at the right end of each branch are the types that appear in reports.

          Three words that overlap: deletion, indel, frameshift.

          Deletion

          Describes what happened to the DNA: bases were removed.

          Indel

          A lab umbrella term for a short insertion, a short deletion, or both together. Many pipelines cap it at about 50 bases, but the limit varies.

          Frameshift

          Describes the effect on the protein: the number of bases lost or gained is not a multiple of 3, so every later codon is read differently.

          A one-base deletion is a deletion, an indel and a frameshift. A 15-base deletion, such as the EGFR exon 19 deletion, is a deletion and an indel, and it keeps the frame. Try it below.

          Illustrative sequence modelled on part of EGFR exon 19 (codons 745 to 760). Changed codons are highlighted. Real reports describe the edit with HGVS, not with pictures.

          Loss does not always mean loss of function. In a tumour suppressor such as TP53 or BRCA1, a frameshift or nonsense variant usually removes the protein, and that is the harm. In an oncogene such as EGFR, an in-frame deletion changes a switch and turns the protein on. MET exon 14 skipping removes a stretch that tags the receptor for destruction, so the receptor builds up and signals more.

          Molecular reports · Classification

          Two different questions: is it harmful, and can we act on it?

          A variant can be clearly harmful and still have no matching drug. A variant can also be actionable in one cancer and meaningless in another. Reports answer two separate questions with two separate scales, and the labels sound alike.

          Is it harmful? Germline variants are classed for disease risk using the ACMG/AMP 2015 system. Somatic variants are classed for whether they drive the cancer, in the ClinGen, CGC and VICC oncogenicity standard of 2022. Can we act on it? Somatic variants are tiered for clinical significance by AMP, ASCO and CAP (2017), and graded for drug evidence by OncoKB and ESCAT.

          Variant source
          Actionability scale
          Classification scales in molecular reports
          ScaleAsksCategories
          ACMG/AMP 2015Does this germline variant cause disease?Pathogenic, likely pathogenic, variant of uncertain significance (VUS), likely benign, benign. "Likely" means more than 90% certainty.
          ClinGen, CGC, VICC 2022Does this somatic variant drive cancer?Oncogenic, likely oncogenic, VUS, likely benign, benign.
          AMP, ASCO, CAP 2017How much clinical weight does this somatic variant carry in this cancer?Tier I strong (Level A: approved therapy or guideline; Level B: well-powered studies with expert consensus). Tier II potential (Level C: approved in another cancer or investigational, with clinical evidence; Level D: preclinical or case reports). Tier III unknown significance. Tier IV benign or likely benign.
          OncoKBHow strong is the evidence for a drug, for this alteration in this cancer?Level 1 (FDA-recognised biomarker for an approved drug in this cancer), 2 (standard care in guidelines, approved drug), 3A (compelling clinical evidence in this cancer), 3B (evidence in another cancer), 4 (compelling biological evidence), R1 (standard-care resistance marker), R2 (compelling clinical evidence of resistance).
          ESCATHow ready is this alteration as a drug target?Tiers I to V and X. Tiers I to IV are split into lettered sub-tiers. I ready for routine use, II investigational but likely, III benefit in other cancers, IV preclinical, V activity without clear benefit, X no evidence.

          The labels collide. "Tier I" means strong clinical significance in the AMP system and ready for routine use in ESCAT. "Level A" is an AMP evidence grade, and "Level 1" is an OncoKB level. They are neighbours, not equivalents. A report that says "pathogenic" about a tumour variant usually means oncogenic, borrowed from the germline vocabulary.

          What a VUS is, and what happens to it.

          1. 1 · ReportedThe lab finds a variant without enough evidence either way.
          2. 2 · Set asideIt is not used to choose treatment or to test relatives.
          3. 3 · Evidence growsPopulation frequency, functional studies, case data and family studies accumulate.
          4. 4 · ReviewedThe lab reclassifies it when the evidence reaches a threshold.
          5. 5 · AmendedAn updated report is issued to the ordering clinician.

          Reclassification is slow and most VUS stay VUS for years. When they move, most move toward benign. In one large commercial laboratory series (Mersch, 2018), about nine in ten reclassified VUS were downgraded to benign or likely benign, and about one in ten was upgraded to pathogenic or likely pathogenic. The same variant can have different labels at different labs, so a date and a lab name matter.

          Molecular reports · Whose DNA is it?

          Whose DNA is it? Germline, somatic or CHIP.

          The same letter change can come from three places. A germline variant is in every cell from birth. A somatic variant arose in the tumour. A CHIP variant (clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential) arose in a blood stem cell and now sits in a growing share of blood cells without being cancer.

          The variant allele fraction (VAF) is the share of sequencing reads that carry the variant. It is the best clue to the source, because each source predicts a different value. Move the sliders to see the expected VAF.

          Tissue sample

          Plasma sample

          Tumour-only and tumour-normal testing

          Tumour-only versus tumour-normal sequencing
          Tumour-onlyTumour-normal
          SequencedTumour DNA alone.Tumour DNA and a matched normal, usually blood or saliva.
          Germline variantsInferred from VAF, population databases and gene lists.Subtracted by direct comparison.
          Weak pointSource is a guess. Rare germline variants can look somatic.Needs the second sample, and consent for any germline findings.

          A tumour-only report may carry a potential germline flag. It means the variant sits in a hereditary cancer gene and has features of an inherited variant, such as a VAF near 50%. It is a prompt, not a result. Confirmation is a separate germline test on blood or saliva, with genetic counselling.

          Why CHIP matters for liquid biopsy

          Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) in plasma comes mostly from blood cells. In healthy people, about 55% comes from white cells and about 30% from red-cell precursors in the bone marrow (Moss, 2018). A blood stem cell clone with a CHIP variant therefore shows up in plasma, even though no cancer is involved.

          The usual CHIP genes are DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1 and JAK2, then PPM1D and TP53. The last two are more common after chemotherapy or radiation. A TP53 or PPM1D variant in plasma that is absent from the tumour is a classic false positive. CHIP is defined by a VAF of at least 2% in blood and becomes more common with age.

          The opposite error also occurs. When a tumour sheds little DNA, the tumour fraction is tiny and a real variant falls below the assay's detection limit. Reports then say "not detected", and guidelines advise tissue testing when plasma is negative.

          Part four · Treatment and response

          Where each treatment reaches, how it kills cancer cells, when it is given, and how response is judged on scans.

          xiii

          Chapter thirteenScale · one site → whole body

          Treatments differ in where they reach and when they are given.

          Surgery and radiation treat a place. Drugs treat the body. Further down, see how each treatment actually kills a cancer cell. Modern therapies blur the line by carrying a payload to wherever a target is found. The same drug can be curative, preventive or palliative depending on when it is used.

          Mechanisms

          How each treatment kills a cancer cell.

          Pick a treatment, then switch it on. Each scene is a simplified diagram of the mechanism, not a picture of real cells.

          Timing words

          Neoadjuvant, adjuvant, definitive. The word depends on what comes first.

          Intent is a separate question. Curative intent means the plan aims for cure; it is not a promise. Palliative cancer treatment aims to control disease or symptoms when cure is not the expected outcome. Supportive palliative care can start at diagnosis and run alongside curative treatment.

          Performance status

          How well can the person manage daily life?

          Before choosing a treatment, the oncologist records one number for overall function. This is the performance status (PS). It is a clinician's judgement of how much the person can do and how much help they need. The most common scale comes from the Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG, 1982) and runs from 0 (fully active) to 5 (dead). The WHO and Zubrod scales use the same steps, so "ECOG PS 2", "WHO PS 2" and "Zubrod 2" mean the same thing in practice. The older Karnofsky scale (KPS, late 1940s) describes similar ground from 100 down to 0 in steps of 10.

          Why one number matters

          Treatment
          Both the choice and the intensity of treatment depend on it. Many regimens are built for people at PS 0 to 1. At PS 2 the options are often narrower or gentler. At PS 3 to 4 treatment is usually limited to supportive care, with exceptions for very sensitive cancers or targeted drugs.
          Trials
          Trial protocols often require ECOG 0 to 1, sometimes 0 to 2. A 2021 ASCO and Friends of Cancer Research working group recommended including people with ECOG PS 2 unless there is a scientific or clinical reason, based on safety, to exclude them.
          Prognosis
          A lower function level is linked to shorter survival in most cancers. Risk models use it: the IMDC model for kidney cancer counts a KPS below 80%.
          Not stage
          Stage describes how far the cancer has spread. PS describes the person. A person with stage IV disease can be PS 0, and a person with stage I disease can be PS 3 because of other illness.

          It is a dated judgement

          PS is assigned by a clinician at a visit, usually in a few seconds, and it changes. It can fall during chemotherapy or after a complication and rise again once the person recovers. A single score without a date tells you little. Two clinicians looking at the same person often differ by one level, and people tend to rate themselves differently from their doctors.

          Eligibility is a window. "ECOG 0-1" in a trial protocol is a rule about who can enter. It describes the trial, and says nothing about the PS of any one person.

          In documents · how performance status is written

          Synthetic Oncology clinic note, 14 Mar 2026

          Assessment: 64-year-old with stage IV adenocarcinoma, on cycle 4. ECOG PS 1 today, was PS 0-1 at baseline. Eligible for trial (requires ECOG 0-2). Rehab notes Karnofsky 80. Previous letter recorded KPS 70%. Referring team wrote WHO PS 2 and good performance status.

          Paediatric clinic note for a different patient, aged 9: Lansky 90.

          Pitfalls when reading a score

          Grading side effects

          CTCAE gives every side effect a name and a grade from 1 to 5.

          The Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) is the National Cancer Institute (NCI) dictionary for naming and grading harms of cancer treatment. An adverse event (AE) is any unfavourable medical occurrence during treatment, whether or not the treatment caused it. Each CTCAE term maps to a term in MedDRA, the international medical dictionary regulators use for safety reporting, so the same event has one name across trials, labels and databases. Each term has its own grade definitions, built on one general pattern.

          Which version?

          v4.03
          Published 2010. Still found in older papers and records.
          v5.0
          Published 27 November 2017. The version behind most trial data, drug labels and papers from 2018 to 2025. It has 26 body-system groups and 837 terms.
          v6.0
          Published 22 July 2025, coded to MedDRA 28.0, with an errata update in January 2026. It is the first release as a spreadsheet with tracked changes. It aims to handle abnormal baseline laboratory values better, refine immunotherapy-related terms and revise several skin terms. NCI set 1 January 2026 as the target for using it in newly opened NCI CTEP and DCP studies; trials already running keep the version in their protocol.
          Check the version. Some cut-points moved between releases. For example, v6.0 grades a neutrophil count of 1,000 to 1,500/mm³ as grade 1, where v5.0 called it grade 2, and v6.0 lowers the grade 4 cut-point from 500 to 100/mm³. A count between the lower limit of normal and 1,500/mm³, grade 1 in v5.0, has no grade in v6.0. The same blood count can carry different grades depending on the version. Data from 2026 onward will mix v5.0 and v6.0. The explorer below uses v5.0, the version most existing data use.

          In documents

          Grades appear as "grade 3 neutropenia", "G3 diarrhoea", "Gr 2 rash", "CTCAE v5.0 grade ≥3", "any-grade" and "grade 1-2". Papers report the worst grade a person had during treatment, which can differ from the grade at any single visit. A grade can come from a lab value, from a clinician's judgement, or from the sponsor's database, and the three do not always agree.

          Two meanings of "grade". Tumour grade (Gleason, Nottingham) describes how abnormal tumour cells look. An adverse event grade describes how bad a side effect is. Neither implies the other. Check for the word "toxicity", "adverse event" or a CTCAE term before reading "grade 3".

          Severity, seriousness and cause

          Severity is not seriousness, and who caused it is a third question.

          Severity is the CTCAE grade: how intense the event is. Seriousness is a separate, regulatory yes-or-no label. An event is a serious adverse event (SAE) if it results in one of the outcomes below, whatever its grade. A grade 3 blood count with no symptoms can be non-serious. A grade 2 event can be serious if it puts the person in hospital. Seriousness triggers faster safety reporting to sponsors and regulators.

          Two traps. Most protocols do not count an admission planned before the study began, or one only to give treatment, as a serious event. And "life-threatening" has a narrower meaning in seriousness rules than a CTCAE grade 4 label: it means the person was at immediate risk of death at the time. An event that might have been fatal had it been worse does not qualify.

          Cause: attribution

          For each event, the investigator also judges whether the treatment caused it. NCI trials use five steps. The call is clinical and can change as more is learned.

          Expectedness

          An event is expected if it is already described in the drug's reference safety information (the investigator's brochure or approved label), with that nature and severity. Otherwise it is unexpected. A serious, unexpected event that is suspected to be caused by the drug is a SUSAR and is reported to regulators on an expedited timeline.

          Immune-related adverse events

          Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) come from checkpoint inhibitors (see the mechanism on checkpoint inhibitors above). Releasing the brakes on T cells can turn them against normal organs. Almost any organ can be affected. The usual targets are skin, gut, liver, hormone glands and lung. The timing is different from chemotherapy toxicity: events often start weeks to months after treatment began, and some appear after it has stopped.

          General principles from the ASCO guideline update (Schneider 2021). The ESMO guideline (Haanen 2022) follows a similar grade-based framework. Organ-specific advice differs, and steroid doses and plans are decided by the treating team. This is education, not a protocol.

          Toxicity and the treatment plan

          How toxicity changes a treatment plan.

          The plan written at the start is a schedule, and side effects rewrite it. Clinicians have four main levers. A delay pushes the next cycle back until the person recovers. A hold pauses a drug, sometimes for several cycles. A dose reduction moves the drug to a lower dose level (written −1, −2) for the rest of treatment, and the dose usually does not go back up. A discontinuation stops a drug for good. Checkpoint inhibitors are generally held or stopped but not dose-reduced; chemotherapy is the drug class that is typically reduced. Step through a synthetic course to see all four.

          Dose intensity in one idea

          Dose intensity is the amount of drug delivered per unit of time, for example mg/m² per week. Relative dose intensity (RDI) divides what was delivered by what the plan intended. Delays, holds and reductions all lower it. Studies in settings such as early breast cancer and aggressive lymphoma have linked an RDI below about 85% to worse outcomes. That figure is a rule of thumb for curative-intent chemotherapy and no universal cut-off, and it matters less where treatment is given to control disease rather than to cure. The stats strip above uses a simple version of RDI for Drug A.

          A dose change is not a new line. Cutting Drug A to level −1, holding Drug B for pneumonitis and restarting both are all still the same line of therapy. A new line starts when the strategy changes, usually after progression or when a different regimen replaces the old one (see "Timing words" above). Exact rules differ between real-world datasets.

          Four ways a course can end

          ReasonHow the note puts itWhat it tells youTrap

          Clinical trials

          How a new treatment earns its place.

          Every standard treatment on this page was once experimental. New treatments are tested in phases. Each phase asks a different question and usually involves more people than the one before.

          Placebos are rare in cancer trials. When an effective treatment exists, people in the comparison group get the current standard treatment, not a dummy pill. A placebo is used only alongside standard care or when no proven treatment exists.

          Chapter fourteenScale · millimetres over months

          Response is measured against two different baselines.

          RECIST 1.1 is the rulebook most solid-tumour trials use to call response or progression on scans. Shrinkage is measured from the start of treatment. Growth is measured from the smallest the disease has ever been. Move the lesions and see the call change.

          Target lesions · longest diameter now

          Beyond RECIST

          Many rulebooks, one question each.

          Every response system asks the same two questions: has the cancer shrunk enough to count as a response, and has it grown enough to count as progression? They differ in what they measure. A scan can give a size or a glow of sugar uptake. A blood test can give a protein or an antigen. A pathologist can give a count of cells left in the specimen.

          The words overlap. CR, PR and PD appear in several systems with different thresholds, so the first job when reading a note is to find which rulebook it used. RECIST 1.1 is the sandbox above. Choose a system below to see what it measures and how it is written in documents.

          PSA over time

          The same blood test, three different rules.

          PSA is a protein made by prostate tissue. After the prostate has been removed it should be almost undetectable. After radiotherapy it falls slowly to a low point called the nadir. On treatment for advanced disease it can fall, hold or climb. What counts as a rise depends on the setting. Choose a setting, then drag the dots or edit the values.

          Synthetic series. Drag a dot up or down to change PSA and left or right to change the date, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. The vertical scale is logarithmic.

          Edit the points

          Trial rules and clinic notes differ. These definitions come from guidelines and trial working groups. A clinic note usually says only "biochemical recurrence" or "PSA progression" and may use a looser or older rule. A PCWG4 update was published in 2026; the PCWG3 thresholds used here are still the ones most documents quote.

          Is any cancer left in the specimen?

          Pathological response after neoadjuvant treatment.

          When treatment is given before surgery, the pathologist examines what remains. The tumour bed is the area where the tumour was, now scar and fibrosis with perhaps some cancer cells left. For breast cancer, the Residual Cancer Burden (RCB) turns five measurements into one index. The index falls into four classes. RCB-0 is a pathological complete response. RCB-III has the worst outlook. Move the sliders or pick a case.

          Where this meets staging. After neoadjuvant therapy the report writes the stage with a yp prefix, for example ypT1c ypN0 (see Chapter x). ypT comes from the largest contiguous focus of invasive cancer, not from the whole tumour bed, so the sliders do not set it. Nodal category follows from the node count and deposit size, and is shown above. RCB-0 matches the breast pCR definition ypT0/is ypN0, which allows in situ cancer to remain.

          pCR is a family of definitions. For breast cancer, the US FDA accepts ypT0/Tis ypN0 (no invasive cancer in breast or nodes) or the stricter ypT0 ypN0 (no invasive or in situ cancer). Rectal trials usually write ypT0 N0. A trial may define pCR in breast alone, in breast and nodes, or in a different way again, so the abbreviation alone does not settle which was used.

          Other breast systems exist. Miller-Payne grades the fall in cellularity against the pre-treatment biopsy, from grade 1 (no change) to grade 5 (no invasive cancer).

          In documents
          "RCB-II", "RCB class II (index 2.7)", "residual cancer burden 3.1", "pCR (ypT0 ypN0)", "near pCR".
          Trap
          A report can say "no residual invasive carcinoma" yet list positive nodes. That is not pCR.
          Trap
          "Complete response" in a clinical note after chemotherapy is a scan or exam finding. pCR is a pathology finding. They often disagree.

          Recurrence vocabulary

          Remission, relapse, progression: which word, when.

          The response system gives a category. The note around it chooses a word for the story. Answer three questions about a patient and see the word most clinicians would use.

          Where
          Local recurrence is in or next to the original site, such as the surgical bed or breast. Regional means the draining lymph nodes. Distant means another organ, also called metastatic recurrence. Staging manuals set organ-specific borders, so a node group that is regional in one cancer can be distant in another.
          How found
          Biochemical means a marker, such as PSA, is rising and nothing is visible. Radiographic means a scan shows it. Clinical means symptoms or examination. One patient can move through all three in order.
          CR, remission, NED
          A complete response is a category under a rulebook. Remission is the haematology and everyday word for the same state. NED (no evidence of disease) means nothing was found on the tests done. It is also used after surgery when no treatment-induced shrinkage ever occurred. NED is not a cure.
          Progression, relapse, refractory
          Progression is growth while on or soon after treatment. Relapse or recurrence is the return of cancer after it could not be detected. Refractory means it never responded or progressed through treatment. Where the cut-off between progression and relapse sits (for example, how many months off therapy) is set by the trial or the disease.
          Mixed response
          Some lesions shrink while others grow. RECIST has no such category. The overall call follows the sums and rules, and the note describes the pattern in words.
          Pseudoprogression
          An apparent increase that is not true growth, later followed by stability or shrinkage. Reported with immunotherapy and in the first months after radiotherapy for glioma. Only a later scan or tissue proves it. See iRECIST and RANO 2.0 above.
          Hyperprogression
          A suspected sharp acceleration of growth after starting immunotherapy. Papers define it differently, often by a jump in growth rate compared with before treatment, so a note using the word is a clinician's impression unless it names a definition.

          Part five · The patient record

          The labels clinicians attach to a cancer as it changes, and how a patient's story becomes dates, lines of therapy and outcomes in real-world data.

          xv

          Chapter fifteenScale · the whole patient

          The labels that choose a treatment.

          Histology says what a cancer is made of, and stage says how far it has spread. Clinicians attach four more kinds of label: a molecular subtype, a sensitivity state, a surgical status and a treatment setting. Each is a separate fact, they appear together in one sentence, and several of them change as the disease does.

          Six labels on one cancer

          One note, six kinds of fact.

          Here is one invented patient with metastatic breast cancer. Each coloured layer answers a different question about the same tumour. Pick a label type to light up its phrases in the clinic note, then select any phrase to see what it means and what it does not.

          Which axis is this word on?

          Why the separation matters. Triple-negative says which receptors are absent. It says nothing about whether the cancer has spread. A model that reads "triple-negative" as a stage, or "platinum-resistant" as a histology, files the fact on the wrong axis and every later step inherits the error.

          Molecular and receptor subtypes

          The same organ can hold very different diseases.

          A subtype is defined by a measurement on the tumour: a receptor, a gene change, a protein level. The measurement is what chooses the drug class. Pick a cancer, then a subtype, to see its definition, the test that defines it, what it implies for treatment and how it is written in documents. Drug names are examples of a class. Chapter xii covers how each test works.

          Shares are approximate and vary by population, stage and test. Prostate cancer has its own state labels (castration-sensitive and castration-resistant) in Chapter ix.

          Can it be removed?

          Resectable describes the tumour. Operable describes the patient.

          Two different questions sit behind the word "surgery". A surgeon reads the scan and asks whether every visible tumour can be taken out, with clear margins, and without sacrificing something that cannot be spared. That is resectability. The anaesthetist and the care team ask whether this person can survive the operation. That is operability. Documents use the words "unresectable" and "inoperable" for different reasons, so choose each answer and read the wording that results.

          The tumour

          The patient

          Worked example: the pancreas.

          Pancreatic cancer is the standard teaching case because its resectability is defined by contact with blood vessels, measured in degrees of the vessel's circumference on a thin-slice CT. The tumour grows beside the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), the coeliac axis, the common hepatic artery (CHA), and the superior mesenteric and portal veins (SMV and PV). An artery cannot be rebuilt as easily as a vein, so the rules for arteries are stricter. Move the sliders. The model follows the NCCN categories for tumours of the head and uncinate process.

          Rules change with the tumour site. Tumours of the pancreatic body and tail have their own criteria: coeliac contact of 180° or less is borderline, and so, in NCCN, is more than 180° without aortic involvement and with an intact, uninvolved gastroduodenal artery, although some panel members would call that locally advanced. Other cancers define resectability differently, so a "borderline resectable" label always needs its organ.

          Words around resectability.

          How it is written in documents

          Sensitivity changes over time

          A sensitivity label is a verdict on the last treatment, not a trait of the tumour.

          Words such as platinum-sensitive, endocrine-resistant and refractory describe how the cancer behaved against a drug class. They are assigned by timing and response, so the same patient carries different labels at different dates. Choose a disease and a course, then step through time. The coloured band shows the label, and the highlighted cards show what changed at each step.

          Prostate cancer follows the same pattern from castration-sensitive to castration-resistant disease. Chapter ix shows those states.

          Other staging systems you will meet

          TNM is not the only way to write a stage.

          Chapters ix and x explained TNM. Several cancers use a different system, and a few of the names that look like stages are really measures of something else. Always note the system, its edition and the year, because the same letter can mean different things.

          SystemWhat it stagesCategoriesWhere you will see it

          Edition matters. FIGO updated its cervical and ovarian systems in 2025, and AJCC editions change T and N cut-offs. A report that says only "stage IIIC" is incomplete without the system and year. Child–Pugh is in the table because it is often written next to a stage, but it measures liver function, and the cancer is staged separately.

          xvi

          Chapter sixteenScale · years of documents → one row of data

          From a patient’s story to real-world data.

          A cancer journey is written down as scans, reports, notes, orders and bills, each with its own date and its own habits of language. Real-world evidence needs one row per patient with dates and events. This chapter shows how the first becomes the second, where the rules are arbitrary, and what the words and codes in those documents mean.

          One patient, many documents

          Every date in real-world data is derived from documents.

          Real-world data (RWD) is health information collected during routine care, not for a study. Nobody records “date of diagnosis” in one box. The date has to be worked out from documents that disagree, arrive late or repeat old text. Below is Case A, extended into a five-year story: resection, recurrence, osimertinib, progression and chemotherapy. Each dot is one synthetic document. Select a derived variable at the bottom to see which documents feed it and why its rule is a choice.

          Outside recordCopied-forward textPartial dateCandidate date

          Lines of therapy

          A line of therapy is computed, not recorded.

          Chapter xiii treated a line of therapy as a clinical decision. In records there is no field called “line”. Only drug administrations exist, and software groups them. Below is one common style of rule set, built from published algorithms. Definitions differ across data vendors, studies and clinical frameworks, so treat each switch as a decision a study team makes and writes down. Flip the switches and watch the same drugs fall into different lines.

          Rules

          Regimen window

          Drugs started within this many days of the first drug belong to one regimen. Hess et al. use 28 days, which covers the first cycle of most chemotherapy given every 21 or 28 days.

          If an earlier drug is still being given, many rule sets call the combination a new line. Clinical frameworks may call it a modified line.

          Every earlier drug stops and a different drug starts.

          Gap longer than

          Published thresholds include 60, 90, 120 and 180 days, sometimes chosen per cancer type. Gap is counted from one administration to the next.

          Fixed in this rule set: dropping one drug from a regimen (de-escalation) stays in the same line. Maintenance, where part of the regimen continues, stays in the same line. Dose changes and a skipped cycle do not start a line.

          Sources for these rules: Hess et al., Future Oncology 2021 (28-day regimen window, gap and add or drop logic); Saini and Twelves, Br J Cancer 2021 (clinical framework); ESMO EnLiST, Ann Oncol 2026; Flatiron Health line-of-therapy documentation. Presets are illustrations of each style, not exact reproductions.

          Real-world endpoints

          Outcomes are measured from an index date until an event or the last sign of life.

          Trials follow every participant on a fixed schedule. Routine care does not. A real-world endpoint borrows a trial idea, such as progression-free survival, and redefines it so it can be read from records. Every patient needs an index date (time zero, often the start of a line of therapy), an event (the thing being timed) or a censoring date (the last time we knew they were event-free). Ten synthetic patients are shown. Switch the endpoint and watch events and censoring move.

          1 · Assessment schedule

          Progression is dated by when someone looked.

          Move the true progression date. A trial scans about every 8 weeks. Routine care scans when the clinician decides to, so detection comes later and in steps.

          2 · Mortality completeness

          A death not recorded is a patient who seems alive.

          An oncology practice sees a death only if it happens there. Hospice, another hospital or home are invisible. Untick “Deaths found by data linkage count” above and survival rises. In one published validation in advanced NSCLC, sensitivity of death capture rose from 66% in structured practice data to 91% after combining sources.

          3 · Informative censoring

          People leave the data when something has changed.

          Patient 8 stopped treatment and stopped appearing. A trial chases such a patient. A database cannot. If people disappear because they are doing worse (or better), censoring carries information and the curve is biased in a direction nobody can see.

          Definitions follow Griffith et al., JCO Clin Cancer Inform 2019 (rwPFS), Ma et al., Adv Ther 2021 (rwR), Curtis et al., Health Serv Res 2018 (mortality) and the Friends of Cancer Research pilots (rwTTD and rwTTNT). For regulators, see the FDA Real-World Evidence Framework (2018) and the FDA guidance on real-world data and evidence for drugs (2023).

          How clinicians write

          The same words can mean the disease is there, was there, may be there or is not there.

          Clinical text is compressed, hedged and full of copied lines. For each mention of a condition, a reader decides three things. Assertion is whether the patient has it. Temporality is when. Certainty is how sure the writer is. Pick a sentence, then turn layers on and off. All sentences are synthetic. The labels blend two published schemes: the i2b2 2010 assertion classes (present, absent, possible, conditional, hypothetical, associated with someone else) and ConText, which records negation, experiencer and temporality (recent, historical, hypothetical) separately.

          Many are ambiguous outside their context. The last column lists the reading to rule out.

          xix

          Chapter nineteenScope

          Sources and limits.

          What this is

          A visual course in cancer for people without a medical background, deep enough for people who build tools that read clinical records: from cells and genes to diagnosis, molecular reports, treatment, toxicity, response and real-world data. All cases, notes and reports are invented.

          What this is not

          Not diagnostic, not a staging calculator, and not treatment advice. Thresholds, editions and drug indications change; check current organ-specific guidance and talk to the care team.

          Editions

          Staging notes follow AJCC 8th-edition concepts, plus Version 9 for lung (in use from 2025). Survival figures are SEER 21, 2016 to 2022. Global figures are GLOBOCAN 2022; IARC released GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates in 2026. US screening advice follows the USPSTF. Adverse events use CTCAE v5.0 (v6.0 noted), response systems follow their published criteria, and prostate risk groups follow NCCN 2025–2026 with earlier groups shown. Checked October 2026.
